chapter: Harlem scene and race in music
title: Playing downtown: dime-a-dance halls and white clubs
summary: Carter describes downtown work with Billy Fowler, dancing schools and small hotel-style groups for white clientele.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Right. But it's interesting about the connection -- this connection between so-called respectable opinion of the black community and jazz, and also a respectable opinion of the white community. Perhaps the black community adopted this attitude because many of these leaders of taste in that community felt that this was the way whites felt. But you played a great deal, I think, in bands that played downtown, and these were for white groups, weren't they?
Well ...
And even in Harlem?

Well, in the early years, like in the 20's when I played with Billy Fowler, that was certainly downtown, at the Cameo Club, and oh, we played someplace else downtown, the names of which escape me at this time. The name, or names -- I don't remember if that was one other place or probably two. But I didn't play with many other

groups downtown; you know, of course Fletcher in the 30's and in the late 20's. Let me see, what else did I do? Prior to that time, I had played downtown but in dancing schools, which was a dime a dance thing, which of course, that was a different thing -- you didn't really have an opportunity to play much jazz, because the emphasis was on the melody of a song and you just played choruses -- one chorus and you'd stop for a couple of seconds and start in to another chorus from another song.
What kind of music was that? Was that what you would call 'hot' music in those days?

Not really, you know. It'd have to be something that was danceable; I mean, you know, these men would come to dance with the hostesses, as I said, for a dime a dance, and many of them were even, in effect, learning to dance, you know, so that it wasn't like the Savoy Ballroom where everybody out there looked like a professional dancer, you know. These were people who were really -- amateurs at dancing, and there was no greatly interesting display of the art of terpsichore. dance.
The dance steps were not exactly a challenge to the musicians?
Right. Not at all. Not at all. Nor, the music to the dancers.
Right.
Yes.

So this would -- I mean how would one compare, say, that kind of music, the music that you played downtown, not just in the dancehalls, to let's say, Paul Whiteman's music. It wasn't symphonic, of course, but ...
No, but it was almost like hotel band music.
I see.

You know, there was usually just a small group, you know, maybe 4 or 5 pieces -- sometimes just a trio, or maybe a trio even, you know? I remember playing a job where I think there was Freddie Johnson on piano, Walter Johnson, who was with Fletcher in later years, on the drums --and me. Just the three pieces. And we just played, you know, a chorus of the current tunes, and ...
Right. And by 'current tunes', you mean the Tin Pan Alley tunes?
Yeah, the Tin Pan Alley tunes, that were known at the moment, you know.
Now would that have been regarded by leaders of the black community as something placing the Negro in a position of a lack of dignity, to be playing that kind of music?
I don't think so -- I don't think there were any members of the black community that ever went in to there, other than the musicians.
Right.
You see, they were all strictly white places, white run and white clientele, you know.
